items.title: Google's AI-generated search summaries reduce clicks to external websites by about 40%, study finds [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
items.summary:
A randomized experiment found that Google's AI-generated Overviews appearing in search results cut clicks to outside websites by nearly 40% among US desktop users. These AI summaries now appear on over 60% of US keywords tracked, up from under 6% two years ago, significantly impacting organic traffic to websites. The study observed that searches with AI Overviews had a higher rate of no outbound clicks, while ad clicks remained stable, indicating Google's revenue was unaffected.

The research, based on a controlled trial and observational data, focused on informational searches and covered desktop users in the US during early 2026. It also noted that the rise of AI Overviews has coincided with declines in traditional featured snippets and forum results. The findings suggest that while SEO remains important, the emergence of generative engine optimization (GEO) is still developing as a strategy to adapt to AI-driven search changes.

items.title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents increased code output by 30% but extended code review time by 49%, shifting the development bottleneck [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
items.summary:
Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from 718 firms using AI coding agents and found that while engineers produced about 30% more code, the time to complete code reviews increased by 49%, resulting in no measurable rise in finished work. Their study, based on data from Jellyfish and LinkedIn employment records, covers activity from January 2021 to March 2026 and uses a staggered difference-in-differences approach to compare early and late adopters of AI tools.

The researchers note that procurement delays and firm size were controlled for in their analysis, and the findings suggest that AI accelerates drafting but shifts the bottleneck to human review stages. The study highlights implications for legal and compliance professionals using AI tools, emphasizing the need to measure approved work product and reviewer time alongside drafting output. The paper is a working paper without completed peer review and focuses on software development rather than legal work.

items.title: Runta and Baseten release FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 leaderboard evaluating 22 harnesses across 5 models and 62 tasks to identify best harness-model pairs by cost and pass rate [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What is the best harness for each model?
items.summary:
Runta partnered with Baseten to create FrontierHarness Eval v1.1, a large-scale benchmark evaluating 22 harness configurations across five AI models and 62 tasks, totaling over 27,000 agent runs and 83 billion tokens. The study aimed to determine whether switching harnesses when changing models improves performance and cost efficiency, finding that the best harness varies significantly by model.

The evaluation measured average cost per task and pass rates, revealing that harnesses optimal for one model may perform poorly with another. For example, Codex CLI was most cost-effective with GLM-5.3 but ranked much lower with other models. The benchmark identified top harnesses for each model based on cost per pass, highlighting trade-offs between cost and accuracy. The results suggest users should consider changing harnesses alongside models to maximize value and performance.

items.title: Researchers identify that continuing reasoning after a correct answer can reduce accuracy in AI models, analyzing commitment-verdict gaps and stopping rules on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
items.summary: Researchers demonstrate that AI reasoning models can lose correct answers by overthinking, as the final verdict alone cannot predict whether continuing reasoning improves or harms accuracy. They introduce a framework comparing the model's current commitment to its final verdict, revealing that the difference predicts potential accuracy changes and informs optimal stopping decisions. Experiments on six reasoning models across MATH-500 and OlympiadBench datasets show that continuing reasoning after a correct answer often decreases accuracy, with an oracle stopping rule providing limited gains. This work clarifies what metrics to measure before designing stopping rules to prevent harmful overthinking in AI reasoning chains.

Experiments on six reasoning models across MATH-500 and OlympiadBench datasets show that continuing reasoning after a correct answer often decreases accuracy, with an oracle stopping rule providing limited gains. This work clarifies what metrics to measure before designing stopping rules to prevent harmful overthinking in AI reasoning chains.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.

items.title: SkillBuffBench benchmark evaluates agent Skills across harnesses, models, skill access modes, and memory on research tasks in materials science and biology [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
items.summary:
SkillBuffBench is a new benchmark and evaluation protocol designed to measure the contribution of agent Skills—file-based procedural knowledge packages—across different agent harnesses, models, skill access modes, and memory settings. It tests state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight models from providers like Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and Chinese companies, running each model under four harnesses on tasks contributed by domain experts in materials science and biology. The benchmark treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, curated Skill, automatic invocation) and evaluates performance with deterministic verification, reporting uncertainty, cost, agent rounds, and wall-clock time alongside scores.

The benchmark's evaluation is ongoing, with results to be added as runs complete and the task suite and analysis updated continuously. This version of the paper details the benchmark's design, evaluation protocol, and current tasks and Skills, aiming to provide a comprehensive and realistic assessment of how agent Skills contribute in deployment scenarios where agents select from installed libraries and retain memory from prior work.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.22017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

items.title: Researchers introduce token commitment as a control surface for steering masked diffusion models, proposing counterfactual target-aware commitment and adaptive budgets to improve target-quality trade-offs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
items.summary:
Researchers propose treating token commitment—the decision of which provisional tokens become permanent and how many to commit at each step—as a control surface for steering masked diffusion models. They introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions based on model confidence and token contribution, and calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. These methods were tested across language and vision-language tasks in the LLaDA family and on the Dream-7B model, showing consistent improvements in target-quality trade-offs and applicability to automatic proxies for task success such as NLI entailment and CLIPScore.

The study demonstrates that these commitment mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on provisional completions, allowing them to function without predefined steering directions. Adaptive schedules also matched or outperformed scorer-free stochastic schedules in terms of denoising cost. The results characterize token commitment as an interpretable and effective control mechanism for masked diffusion generation under the tested conditions.

These methods were tested across language and vision-language tasks in the LLaDA family and on the Dream-7B model, showing consistent improvements in target-quality trade-offs and applicability to automatic proxies for task success such as NLI entailment and CLIPScore.

The study demonstrates that these commitment mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on provisional completions, allowing them to function without predefined steering directions. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

items.title: Researchers analyze 14 language models to distinguish moral evaluation circuits from cue word responses using 227 phrase pairs across moral and normative judgments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
items.summary:
Researchers studied 14 open-weight language models, including Llama, Gemma, and Qwen, to identify attention heads and sparse autoencoder features that influence moral judgments in prompts. They tested 227 minimal phrase pairs differing in moral standards, other norms, or descriptive qualities, with and without the word "morally," finding that the same evaluation circuits handle moral and other normative judgments equally across models.

The study showed these evaluation heads are essential even when no explicit judgment is requested, significantly affecting model responses on the ETHICS benchmark scenarios. Sparse autoencoder features primarily responded to the presence of the word "morally" rather than the phrase content. The models encode normative categories in their hidden states, and removing these directions weakens moral verdicts more than other judgments in most tested models. The researchers released their data, code, and trained models for further analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

items.title: Researchers introduce EJBench, a software-agnostic benchmark testing engineering judgement on conjugate heat transfer design for battery cold plates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
items.summary: EJBench evaluates whether models can predict design behavior under new conditions using limited prior results, without running simulations. The benchmark includes tasks such as matching unlabelled test results to operating points, selecting stored runs for design approval, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature, all based on converged simulation data rather than language model judgement. The best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, achieved a score of 0.71, while post-training Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning improved its score from 0.071 to 0.106 on a held-out test set. The researchers have released the dataset splits, evaluation tools, and leaderboard to support further development and comparison.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21707v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

items.title: Researchers profile and optimize the sampling pipeline in 26B-parameter MoE diffusion language models, achieving up to 2.7x decoding speedup on NVIDIA GB10 without accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
items.summary: Researchers analyzed the decoding process of a 26-billion-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model on a bandwidth-limited NVIDIA GB10 edge accelerator and found that after weight quantization, the logits sampling pipeline, rather than expert GEMMs, dominated decode time. Unlike autoregressive models, diffusion decoding processes multiple times more logits per output token due to iterative denoising steps. The team developed two lossless optimizations—a bit-exact tier and an accuracy-parity tier using fused entropy kernels and Gumbel-max sampling—that removed redundant computations and improved decoding speed by 2.4 to 2.7 times without affecting benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH datasets.

Unlike autoregressive models, diffusion decoding processes multiple times more logits per output token due to iterative denoising steps. The team developed two lossless optimizations—a bit-exact tier and an accuracy-parity tier using fused entropy kernels and Gumbel-max sampling—that removed redundant computations and improved decoding speed by 2.4 to 2.7 times without affecting benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH datasets.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.

items.title: Researchers introduce Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model to capture document and section hierarchies in embedding space, improving topic coherence and clustering across structured text collections [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
items.summary: Researchers present the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that links topic distributions of documents and their sections through a hierarchical prior in embedding space. This approach addresses the limitation of traditional embedded topic models that represent each document with a single topic distribution, ignoring internal hierarchical structure common in legal documents, reports, and forums. The team developed an amortized variational inference method for hETM and tested it on various structured datasets. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity compared to flat and hierarchical baselines, with comparable or better topic quality. It also outperforms other models in downstream clustering tasks on most collections, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling hierarchical document structures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.21980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.

items.title: Researchers propose RLDE, a reinforcement learning framework for interpretable iterative document editing that improves readability and preserves semantics with low computational cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
items.summary: Researchers introduce RLDE, an end-to-end reinforcement learning framework that models document revision as a Markov decision process using limited editing actions and optimizes for readability, perplexity, and grammar without relying on paired revision targets. RLDE employs Pointer Networks for token-level span selection and a frozen BART-base model for context-aware suggestions, with a novel semantic preservation penalty to maintain meaning during edits. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset show significant improvements in readability and perplexity while preserving 93% of semantic content, outperforming Chain-of-Thought prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 at a lower inference cost. Human evaluations rated RLDE's edits highly for meaning preservation and quality.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.22039v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. In this paper, we propose RLDE, an automated end-to-end metric-driven RL framework that formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP problem (unsupervised with respect to paired document-revision targets). Working with a limited action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), RLDE leverages Pointer Networks for dynamic span selection at the token level and sends generative actions to the frozen BART-base model to obtain context-aware suggestions. PPO agents learn to optimize a multi-objective reward function based on readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics with the help of a novel SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty constraint to avoid deletion degeneracy. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset showed statistically significant results (p < 0.01) across all metrics, where Flesch Reading Ease increased from 49.8 to 59.4, perplexity decreased from 63.7 to 39.8, while preserving 93% of semantic information. When compared to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, RLDE shows high performance at a very low computational inference cost. Moreover, the quality of edits generated by RLDE has been verified via human evaluations, scoring 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality.

items.title: Researchers show large language models can design efficient weight-space programs without transformers, achieving comparable accuracy with far fewer parameters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
items.summary:
Researchers explored weight-space programming where large language models (LLMs) generate neural network weights directly without gradient-based training, questioning the necessity of transformer architectures. They tasked three advanced LLMs with either generating weights for fixed architectures or designing architectures themselves, mainly on multiple-choice question tasks. When allowed to design freely, the LLMs created sparse table-based models that reached up to 54.4% test accuracy, outperforming transformer models written by the same LLM while using about 1,800 times fewer parameters.

The study found that without gradients, LLMs preferred associative-memory-based models that allow explicit interpretation and correction of weights, leading to models up to 17 times faster on GPUs than similarly sized transformers. While pretrained LLMs remain more accurate overall, the findings suggest alternative architectures may be more suitable for weight-space programming where weights are written directly rather than trained with gradients.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.22055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

items.title: NVIDIA post-trains Nemotron 3.5 Super with reinforcement learning on expert-built tasks, improving performance across 12 benchmarks including software engineering and document reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
items.summary:
NVIDIA applied reinforcement learning to post-train its Nemotron 3.5 Super model using five expert-built task datasets covering software engineering, complex constraints, tool use, chart understanding, and document reasoning. Each training run used a fresh LoRA adapter without supervised stages, and the adapters were evaluated against the base model on the same tasks and settings, showing significant performance gains on twelve benchmarks.
The improvements ranged from 4.5 to 13.8 points across various benchmarks such as IFBench, GDP_pdf, SWE-bench Pro V2, Terminal-Bench 2.1, MultiChallenge, AutomationBench, and Chartography. The adapters demonstrated enhanced capabilities like better data and rule identification, test file generation, context retention, precise chart measurement, and spreadsheet reading compared to the base model.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.22161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.

items.title: OfficePrism benchmarks AI agents on 420 single-domain enterprise tasks across seven business functions with pass rates from 22.6% to 76.4% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OfficePrism: Benchmarking Agents on Single-Domain Operations Across Enterprise Business Functions
items.summary: OfficePrism evaluates AI agent performance on 420 single-domain tasks spanning seven enterprise business functions, using a shared synthetic organization and function-specific domains. The benchmark includes tasks structured at three levels (L1-L3) and uses a pipeline that generates Chinese-language tickets, executable reference witnesses, and expected responses, followed by automated filtering and human curation. Across 124 model and package configurations, pass rates vary from 22.6% to 76.4%, with the highest success at the simplest task level (L1) and better performance at level 2 compared to level 3 in most cases. The study compares full-schema and search-and-dispatch evaluation packages, finding search outperforms full-schema in 30 of 50 comparable configurations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.22262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Broad workplace scores can mix competence within one business function with the extra cost of coordinating across functions and systems, making failures hard to localize. OfficePrism evaluates this prerequisite through 420 single-domain enterprise tasks spanning seven business functions under shared, benchmark-defined L1--L3 task-structure levels. Each task runs in a fresh environment combining a shared synthetic organization with one function-specific domain and yped state access. Our pipeline uses grounded records, business rules, and tool schemas to jointly construct a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference witness, and an expected response, followed by automated filtering and human curation. The same task set is evaluated through full-schema and search-and-dispatch packages. Across 124 model--harness--package configurations, the per-case joint natural-language-and-database pass rate ranges from 22.6% to 76.4%, with a median of 67.9%. L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, and L2 exceeds L3 in 122. Among 50 configurations sharing the same harness and model labels across both packages, search scores higher in 30, ties in one, and scores lower in 19.

items.title: Researchers introduce ICA Lens to identify interpretable non-Gaussian directions in language model activations, demonstrating efficiency and competitive performance across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ICA Lens: Non-Gaussianity Reveals Interpretable Directions in Language Models
items.summary: Researchers developed ICA Lens, a workflow that directly discovers non-Gaussian directions in large language model residual-stream activations without training sparse dictionaries. Testing on GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, they found these directions capture coherent lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns, correlating with human and automated interpretability measures. ICA Lens achieves comparable results to sparse autoencoders while using significantly less memory and computation time, highlighting non-Gaussianity as a direct unsupervised signal for interpretable feature discovery in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.11722v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finding human-interpretable directions in language-model activations is important for understanding and controlling model behavior. These directions are usually discovered through indirect learning objectives such as sparse reconstruction, but it remains unclear what existing statistical structure distinguishes interpretable directions and whether that structure can be used directly for feature discovery. We find that non-Gaussianity provides such a signature: projection distributions of natural-text residual-stream activations along sparse autoencoder (SAE) decoder directions are substantially more non-Gaussian than those along random directions, with most contexts forming a concentrated background and recurring patterns often occupying one tail. This raises a natural question: if interpretable directions tend to have non-Gaussian projection distributions, can we discover them by searching for non-Gaussian directions directly in activation space, without training another sparse dictionary? To test this hypothesis, we introduce ICA Lens, a practical workflow for efficient discovery, reliable annotation, and faithful evaluation of non-Gaussian directions in LLM residual-stream activations. Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, we find that (1) the recovered non-Gaussian directions capture coherent lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns under both human and LLM-based evaluation; (2) non-Gaussianity is positively associated with both human-label confidence and automated interpretability; and (3) the resulting coordinates are competitive with SAEs across interpretability, sparse reconstruction, concept prediction, and causal interventions, while fitting in minutes per layer and using 7-43 times less memory. These results show that non-Gaussianity is a direct unsupervised signal for discovering interpretable and useful structure in activations.

items.title: Researchers introduce Localized LoRA-MoE combining spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing to improve parameter-efficient fine-tuning across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Localized LoRA-MoE: Mixture of Low-Rank Experts With Adaptive Routing
items.summary:
Researchers present Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that integrates localized spatial blocking with adaptive, context-conditioned routing to address gradient interference in parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA. They propose two variants—Block-Wise LoRA-MoE with centralized routing and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE with decentralized routing—and evaluate them on structured transformation benchmarks, showing improved performance over static baselines under similar adapter budgets.
The study demonstrates that both variants perform comparably when context shifts uniformly, while cell-wise routing excels in spatially heterogeneous contexts. Fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing outperforms LoRA and static adapters at fixed budgets, matching per-task adapters with six times the budget. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both variants surpass static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving a 3.9-point improvement over LoRA at matched active capacity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05114v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA adapt large models through a single low-rank update. Such updates are susceptible to gradient interference: when a training stream interleaves multiple operational contexts, conflicting updates to shared adapter weights collapse the adapter into an unspecialized average. While recent methods introduce block-wise isolation to remedy this issue, their topologies are static and cannot adapt to context switching or localized sensor degradation. In this work, we introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that combines localized spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing. We propose and evaluate two architectural variants: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE (centralized routing), which modulates the entire structural grid through a single context-conditioned gate, and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE (decentralized routing), which assigns an independent gate to every coordinate cell of the matrix grid. Across three structured transformation benchmarks--a high-dimensional SVD matrix simulation, context-switched transformations over real tabular data, and spatial reconstruction under simulated sensor occlusion--both variants outperform static baselines under comparable adapter budgets. Both variants perform similarly when context shifts the grid uniformly, while cell-wise routing is strictly better when contexts are spatially heterogeneous. When fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing at a fixed adapter budget outperforms LoRA and static localized adapters, matching per-task adapters with 6x budgets. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both routed variants outperform static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving +3.9 points over LoRA at matched active capacity.

items.title: Researchers identify simulator collapse in multi-agent reinforcement learning with single LLM simulators and propose Verbalized Sampling and Co-Training to improve generalization and policy diversity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
items.summary:
Researchers found that multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) agents trained against a single large language model (LLM) simulator often fail to generalize due to simulator collapse, where the simulator exhibits mode collapse and the agent learns narrow strategies that do not transfer well to other simulators or real users. They formalized this issue and proposed two solutions: Verbalized Sampling, which samples simulator replies from a response distribution at inference time, and Co-Training, which co-evolves the simulator and policy during training to prevent exploitation of mode behavior.

The team validated these methods on three benchmarks—Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench—showing that Verbalized Sampling improved held-out success rates by up to 9%, while Co-Training increased gains to 14%, with similar improvements observed in a human study. items.originalTitle: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
items.summary: Researchers developed SarcasTraps, a dataset of 479 Turkish entries annotated for hate speech and sarcasm, to study how sarcasm affects hate speech detection. They trained classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on existing datasets and tested them alongside GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in zero-shot settings. The results show sarcasm significantly reduces recall in fine-tuned models and lowers precision in zero-shot large language models, indicating both struggle with sarcastic hate speech. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.16957v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.

items.title: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. One risk is that models could deliberately shape their reasoning to make it opaque to monitors. We stress-test this risk through persona-control training: supervised fine-tuning on mathematical reasoning traces rewritten in the voices of diverse personas. This induces a broader ability to control CoT, even though training contains no monitor-evasion examples. In covert side-task evaluations, traces in which a gpt-oss-20b model organism completes the hidden side task contain less monitorable evidence than the base model's. Averaged across evaluations and CoT lengths, weighted by side-task-success counts, the CoT monitorability metric g-mean$^2$ falls from 0.94 for the base model to 0.68 for the model organism without a hiding instruction, and to 0.22 when explicitly instructed to hide. In intervention evaluations, explicit hiding often drives monitorability near zero. The effect extends to a Kimi-K2.6 model organism in agentic environments, though hidden objectives requiring extended reasoning or longer trajectories remain more monitorable than simple single-step side tasks. We further discover that targeted transparency prompts can substantially recover monitorability, sometimes surpassing the base model. These model organisms provide a testbed for studying monitorability failures and potential mitigations. Our code can be found on https://github.com/yongzx/cot-control-model-organism.

items.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

items.title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

items.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. items.title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

items.title: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LoCaR: Localized Canvas Retrieval With Frozen Vision-Language Model
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whole image embeddings can under represent small objects and local attributes that distinguish relevant images for localized queries. We present LoCaR, a training free framework for localized text to image retrieval with frozen vision language models. LoCaR constructs and utilizes independent proposals (SAM2) focusing on the object so as to get a more localized representation that independently encodes each region using the frozen visual encoder. We further study paired-support adaptation as an optional residual that uses matched text region exemplars without updating the underlying encoders. We also introduce LOCFG, a Visual Genome derived benchmark designed to evaluate localized retrieval for smaller and more challenging referents. Across several vision language backbones, our results show that improving the region representation itself is the main source of gain.

items.title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat) [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.

items.title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.

items.title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. items.title: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multistage Contextual Optimization for Vehicle Repositioning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms reposition idle vehicles to improve spatial supply-demand balances. This problem is prediction-driven and multistage: at each stage, the platform forecasts future demand, executes current decisions, and uses the resulting state to initialize the next stage. We formulate a multistage linear program (LP) with a macroscopic fundamental diagram (MFD) linking accumulation to trip completion. We then develop a multistage contextual optimization approach that uses decision performance to train the prediction model. The learning problem combines multiple coupled stages, context that depends on earlier decisions, and predictions that affect the objective, the constraint matrix, and the right-hand side of the LP. We derive the exact gradient, which has three parts: parameters change forecasts and hence decisions; earlier decisions change the current decision through the inherited state; and this state also changes forecasts as context. An equivalent adjoint uses reverse vector-Jacobian products, avoiding full solution and state-parameter Jacobians. Finally, forward propagation solves many stage LPs one after another, which makes training slow. We propose a parallel block evaluation algorithm that solves blocks of consecutive stages in parallel and repeatedly feeds each block output to the next block. We prove that the algorithm recovers the serial trajectory within a finite number of passes and that its gradient error remains bounded when it stops early. On New York City ride-hailing data, multistage contextual optimization yields 7.7% to 9.1% more business benefit than the same predictor trained by mean squared error, outperforms all compared baselines from five paradigms, and even outperforms realized demand fed to the same policy. With eight workers, parallel block evaluation shortens training by a factor of 1.86 without loss of decision performance.

items.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.

items.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

items.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

items.title: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PACT: Plan-Action Consistency Training by Preserving Correct Plans and Repairing Actions in GUI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GUI agents can formulate a correct immediate plan in their reasoning yet emit an action that fails to execute it, creating an execution gap. This recurring mismatch undermines reliable task completion, as a single execution error can derail a multi-step workflow. In outcome-supervised reinforcement learning, broadcasting a negative response-level advantage across all generated tokens risks penalizing valid planning together with erroneous execution. Using annotated reference actions to identify execution gaps, PACT protects the verified plan by masking negative policy-gradient contributions across its token span. Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

items.title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
items.summary: arXiv:2611.22597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.

items.title: Improved Convergence Rates for Stochastic Multi-Gradient Descent which Close the Gap: A Proof by AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improved Convergence Rates for Stochastic Multi-Gradient Descent which Close the Gap: A Proof by AI
items.summary: arXiv:2607.18174v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMG) computes an approximate steepest common descent direction of the objectives from stochastic gradients. Under standard assumptions, this note establishes a new convergence rate for SMG in terms of the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared empirical PS measure at the algorithm's output is $\tilde{O}(T^{-1})$ after $T$ iterations. This improves on the $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/4})$ bound obtained by Chen et al. (JMLR, 2024) for linearly growing batches, without requiring bounded gradients. Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The key to the rate improvement is to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure, defined by the norm of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) direction, rather than the $(1/2)$-H\"older continuity of the MGDA direction used by Chen et al. (2024). For variants of MoCo and MoCo+ with exact MGDA updates and constant batch sizes, the analysis gives expected squared empirical PS rates of $O(T^{-1/2})$ and $\tilde{O}(T^{-2/3})$, respectively. These bounds match the corresponding single-objective momentum rates up to logarithmic factors. The proof was accidentally discovered while the author was preparing homework for a graduate course: ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended generated the initial proof strategy for the main SMG result in response to an author-written homework-solution prompt; the author then verified and reorganized the resulting argument. The appendices document the prompt, summarize the student submissions with LLM disclosures, and present additional proofs and results on momentum-based stochastic MGDA.

items.title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

items.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.

items.title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

items.title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.21650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.
